paper_title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To optimize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objective. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea's quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. We show that our trained 8B model achieves higher creative utility (a measure combining quality and diversity) than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on our contamination-free benchmark. In a pilot human study with four experts, our sets are judged as promising as Claude Opus 4.8's and contain marginally more unique ideas. When a coding agent runs proof-of-concept experiments on the ideas, our model's success@k is comparable to Claude Opus 4.8's, so we see that the added diversity does not cost any executability.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The first step of any research cycle is generating ideas worth testing, before an experiment can tell you which one was right. Current work with Large Language Models (LLMs) on idea generation has focused on one of two things: producing single idea and scoring it against an existing, held-out idea (He-Yueya et al., 2026), or building end-to-end systems that carry one idea through execution and judge whether that execution succeeded (Kirgis et al., 2026; Ning et al., 2026; Falck et al., 2026; Garikaparthi et al., 2026; Si et al., 2026). Either way, an idea is generated and judged on its own, never alongside other candidates it could be weighed against. Looking at how humans do research, researcher facing body of literature brainstorms several directions off the same shared context, and then selects among them using some signal (Platt, 1964; Klahr & Dunbar, 1988), rather than just committing to one idea. We draw connection between ideation and creative problem solving. The brainstorm-then-select process is how creative thinking/problem solving can also be formalized, divergent thinking explores space broadly for many candidates, and convergent thinking narrows it through selection (Boden, 2004; Guilford, 1967). The way current LLMs are used for ideation can look different. Because each idea is generated and judged on its own, multiple candidates come from repeated independent sampling, with no shared context to explore deliberately and no pool to converge over. Any diversity among them is incidental rather than designed (Puri et al., 2026; Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026). Work on autonomous research agents has also flagged diversity as shortcoming (Liu et al., 2026; Garikaparthi et al., 2026). Also Work done while at Salesforce AI Research. 1Code and data: https://github.com/ManyaWadhwa/diverge_ideation 1 Preprint. Under Review. Figure 1: Overview of our training pipeline. Given set of documents, the policy generates set of ideas = {u1, . . . , uk}; for reasoning models, the whole set is generated after single shared reasoning prefix. Each idea ui is scored by its quality qi and its distance di to the closest earlier idea (d1 = 1), giving per-item reward ri = qi di. The set reward R(U ) = (cid:80) ri is used as the RL signal to update the policy, encouraging sets that are both high-quality and diverse. previous attempts at training an ideation model against execution signal has been shown to collapse onto single dominant idea rather than spread of them (Si et al., 2026). In our work, we close this gap by treating idea generation as creative search problem. Given corpus of prior documents, an agent should propose set of ideas, each grounded in specific source documents, that are high-quality and differ from each other by design. We study this for documentgrounded ideation (Wang et al., 2024). We combine quality and diversity into one set-level training signal by adapting the Creative Utility formulation (Wadhwa et al., 2026) where each idea earns credit for its own quality and for its distance from the ideas emitted before it, so redundant idea earns little no matter how well-written it is (as illustrated in Figure 1). To achieve this, we train an ideation model (Qwen3-8B (Team, 2025)) in two steps. We first do supervised fine-tuning step to initialize the policy on well-formed idea sets, followed by GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) against set-level objective (adapted from the creative utility formulation). We then report this utility measure on contamination-free test set that we put together. We also look at two existing benchmarks, GiantsBench (He-Yueya et al., 2026) and IdeaSeed (Chen et al., 2026). Our tested baselines include the untrained base model and its SFT checkpoint, strong closed-source agents, GIANTS (He-Yueya et al., 2026), and DARLING (Li et al., 2025), an alternative qualitydiversity objective that we retrain in our setting. We show that our 8B trained model achieves the highest creative utility on our test set, outperforming strong closed-source agents and competing quality-diversity objectives such as DARLING. small pilot human study with four expert annotators finds that our sets are comparable to Claude Opus 4.8s in the number of promising ideas, while containing more mutually distinct ones. Finally, when we execute each set of ideas in fixed sandbox with coding agent, our model is comparable to Claude Opus 4.8 on success@k, showing that we are able to increase diversity without compromising important aspects of ideation like executability. Contributions Our contributions are (1) set-level RL objective for training that balances quality and diversity; (2) an instantiation of this objective for document-grounded ideation; and (3) an 8B trained ideation model that outperforms strong closed-source agents and models trained on competing objectives on creative utility, and whose ideas are comparably promising in small pilot human and execution study.

sections.title: 2.1 BACKGROUND
sections.content: We start by describing the standard reinforcement learning setting for language models we build on. policy parameterized as an LM πθ maps prompt to distribution over textual outputs y. Given reward function R(x, y) R, training aims to maximize expected reward: ExD, yπθ(x) (cid:2)R(x, y)(cid:3). max θ (1) Preprint. Under Review. We optimize Equation 1 with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024): for each x, we sample rollouts {y1, . . . , yG} πθ( x), score each with R(x, yg), and update the policy using each rollouts advantage relative to the groups mean reward, with no learned critic.

sections.title: 2.2 SET-LEVEL OBJECTIVE
sections.content: In our setting, each prompt is answered by set of outputs = {u1, . . . , uK} written in single generation, after shared reasoning prefix. This set is the rollout in Eq. 1, so GRPO scores it with one scalar and computes one advantage per set. All outputs therefore share that single credit signal. Our goal is set that is high-quality and whose outputs are mutually distinct. Then we train the model using set-level objective using the definition below: Rset(x, ) = (cid:88) i=1 q(ui) min j<i d(ui, uj), min j<i d(ui, uj) := 1 if = 1 (2) For each item in the generation, we multiply its quality by how far it is from its nearest predecessor and aggregate over the set to get the reward. redundant but high quality item earns almost nothing (Fig 1). The objective has two components: quality function q(ui) [0, 1] that scores an output for the prompt, and distance d(, ) [0, 1] between two outputs. Any task with quality signal and notion of diversity fits, such as instruction following, creative writing, or ideation; we instantiate both for document-grounded ideation in Section 3.1. Relation to Creative Utility. Eq. 2 is adapted from Creative Utility (CU) (Wadhwa et al., 2026), which scores set of ideas by the quality each one adds beyond the ideas already selected. We make two design choices in adapting it to training reward. First, CU applies patience discount (γ) to later ideas; we drop it for training, so every idea in the set is weighted equally and model cannot fall back on generating weak ideas later in the set. Second, CU takes the best ordering of the set; we instead use the order in which the model writes them. Our prompt asks the model to list ideas from most to least promising, and it lets the reward be computed directly from single rollout. At evaluation we report CU as is (Section 4). Relation to multi-answer RL. Our proposed objective can be viewed as generalized form of the set-level objective introduced by Puri et al. (2026). Their formulation however has no notion of distance and instead only checks for coverage against an established ground truth answer set. Their objective can be defined as special case of Eq 2, by setting d(ui, uj) = 1 and to coverage metric.

sections.title: 3 DOCUMENT GROUNDED IDEATION
sections.content: As mentioned in Section 1, we study the task of document-grounded ideation i.e. given body of related literature, an agent needs to generate set of ideas worth pursuing next, and we evaluate the set of ideas for its quality and diversity. Task definition. An instance is corpus of documents = {d1, . . . , dn} (each scientific paper, given as summary). An agent must produce set of ideas = {u1, . . . , uK}, where each idea ui is structured idea card with four fields: problem gap, core claim, method, and an inspiration field that names the specific source documents the idea draws on and how. Why set of K? We make the set the primary unit, generating all ideas in one pass so each is written conditioned on those already emitted. The agent can actively avoid repeating itself, steering later ideas toward directions its earlier ones left uncovered, rather than relying on independent draws to spread apart by chance (Puri et al., 2026; Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). See Appendix A.1 for definitions of the idea card sub fields and examples of ideas.

Quality: part of ideation is to come up with directions that are worth pursuing next, so we define quality as long-term scientific impact (Tong et al., 2026). While there are other properties of good ideas such as fluency or soundness, these are not sufficient to decide if the idea is worth pursuing next. We therefore treat soundness as separate axis, which we only probe with small execution check (Section 6.2), rather than the training target. We anchor long-term impact to the gold idea g, reference idea whose value is already established, so the judgment reflects what the field found worth doing. Section 3.2 describes how we obtain g. Distance captures whether two ideas represent different directions. Two ideas can share problem while having completely different methods. We operationalize this metric by scoring semantic distance field-wise over the problem gap, claim, and method fields, using an LLM-judged similarity rubric, and averaging with equal weight across the three fields. d(ui, uj) = 1 3 (cid:0)dproblem(ui, uj) + dclaim(ui, uj) + dmethod(ui, uj)(cid:1), (4) where each dfield [0, 1] is per-field distance derived from 15 LLM-judged similarity rubric and normalized to be in the [0, 1] range. For impact reward we use an off-the-shelf reward model, SciJudge-30B (Tong et al., 2026) and for distance we use gpt-oss-120b (OpenAI, 2025). sections.title: 3.2 DATA
sections.content: We build training set and contamination-free test set from published papers. Our data construction pipeline has two steps: (a) gathering the source and target documents (b) generating data for supervised fine-tuning. Each instance pairs target paper (or gold idea) with its source documents. Gathering documents. We take each paper in the training split of GiantsBench (He-Yueya et al., 2026) as target and retrieve its full text and citation graph, including the in-text context of each citation. An LLM (claude-sonnet-4-6) selects the source documents from the targets references, keeping those that motivated the paper, exposed the gap it addresses, supplied its conceptual foundation, or were directly extended (Cohan et al., 2019). Each source is summarized into source card in the idea-card schema, and the cards form the input corpus D. The targets text is summarized into an idea card and held out as the gold idea g. We drop instances with two or fewer source documents or no gold idea. For training we focus on the Language domain. The test set is built using the same pipeline but with target papers 2026 (Section4). The test split also spans 16 domains (distribution in Figure 5, Appendix A). SFT data construction The SFT stage teaches the idea-card format and thinking pattern. teacher LLM (claude-opus-4.8) first proposes ideas from the source documents alone. Because we cannot access closed models reasoning, we then use hindsight prompting, where the teacher sees the sources and its own ideas and writes first-person exploration that arrives at exactly those ideas, floating and rejecting candidates, hedging over the sources and raising questions. Each instance gets different opening statement so traces do not collapse into one template. We train on 7,172 instances and use 1,740 for testing. Appendix has details about the train and test splits.

sections.title: 3.3 TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: Our proposed training setup has two steps: (a) light supervised fine-tuning with next token prediction to teach the model the format of our task as well as the thinking pattern, and, (b) GRPO as the base RL algorithm. We use Qwen3-8B (Team, 2025) as the base model with maximum response length of 16k tokens, and we set = 3. We repeat these two steps for two setups of training: (i) with 4 Preprint. Under Review. think: where we optimize for the thinking traces that we constructed in the previous section and (ii) no think: where we only optimize for the final answer block and have an empty think block. We also show the recipe generalization on Olmo-3-7B-Think-SFT (Olmo et al., 2025). The hyperparameters, SFT variants, Olmo-3 details and compute details are in Appendix B.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Baselines. We compare model trained with our proposed objective against four groups of systems. General models. We evaluate strong closed-source models (Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra) and representative open-source model (Nemotron-120B (NVIDIA, 2025)), prompted zero-shot with our set-generation prompt. Competing objectives. DARLING (Li et al., 2025) is the closest approach to ours that optimizes quality and diversity together, but across the rollouts of single-idea policy rather than within the generated set. We replicate the algorithm for our task and train it with = 1, so the only difference from our method is where diversity is enforced (Appendix B.3). Impact-only RL uses our set-level RL setup with the diversity term removed (i.e., = 1 in Eq. 2), and isolates what the diversity term contributes. Impact+diversity, no SFT uses our full reward but starts GRPO directly from the base model, and isolates what the SFT warm-start contributes. These are trained from the same base model and training corpus as our method. Base and SFT. Qwen3-8B (base) is the untrained base model, prompted for ideas directly. SFT is the checkpoint after supervised initialization and before GRPO. Both are the starting points for our method. Proposed. Proposed is SFT followed by GRPO with our set-level reward (Eq. 2). For SFT and Proposed we report two variants: think and no think. Benchmarks. We evaluate the above on three datasets. 1. Ours (contamination-free). GiantsBench (He-Yueya et al., 2026). The input for this dataset is two documents. sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: Proposed (no think) achieves the highest Creative Utility Table 1, shows that the proposed model trained with the set-level reward and no thinking, Proposed (no think), achieves the highest creative utility and win-rate, with high distance between ideas. This utility increases from 0.03 (base model), to 0.21 (SFT no think) to 0.64 post our proposed training (no think). We also beat state of the art closed source models, where Claude Opus 4.8 achieves CU of only 0.38 and GPT-6 Astra achieves 0.28. The thinking variant of our proposed training, Proposed (think) achieves utility of 0.51, which still beats both closed-source models but is lower than the no-think variant and on par with DARLING (0.52) and the no-SFT ablation (0.51). We discuss this trade-off at the end of this section. The high creative utility is because both impact against gold (win-rate) and idea diversity are high for our proposed model. Full table in Appendix E. Proposed training recipe beats different competing objectives Training with set level objective for only quality (Impact-only RL) gives good win-rate (43%), but it collapses the set. Its average distance falls to 0.38. This shows that training for quality only in set can get us good ideas, but the model ends up focusing on only one good instead of trying to get multiple good ideas. For DARLING, we see that it reaches utility of 0.52 against 0.64 for Proposed (no think), but has lower distance (0.67 against 0.88). Showing that rewarding within-set generation for diversity is more effective than across-rollout diversity. SFT keeps the model grounded To test the SFT warm-start, we train the same base model with our objective but skip SFT (Impact+diversity, no SFT). This baseline matches Proposed (think) at 0.51 CU, but does worse on grounding as seen in Figure 2. Grounding for the no SFT baseline falls to = 0.19, against 0.81 with SFT (Figure 2). Without the warm-start, the policy gets its diversity by drifting away from its source documents. It also stays 0.13 CU below Proposed (no think). So SFT is what lets the set-level reward raise utility without losing grounding. 6 Preprint. Under Review. Thinking helps retain grounding Proposed (think) has lower utility than Proposed (no think) (0.51 vs. 0.64). Primary reason for this is lower win rate (0.34 vs. 0.50), but we see that thinking gets more grounding (0.81 vs. 0.61; Figure 2). The grounding gap appears only after RL, since SFT-only think and no-think models are equally grounded (0.91 vs. 0.90). Thinking thus seems to help the policy retain grounding as RL pushes for utility. We hypothesize two reasons why thinking may not raise utility. First, the reward scores only the final ideas, and the impact signal is judged comparison against gold idea that cannot be verified at intermediate steps. Thus the steps might not have enough causal influence on the reward (Sprague et al., 2025). Second, designing thinking traces suitable for creative ideation is an open-problem. In our work, we tried one approach that was hindsight generation. While we instruct the teacher model to propose negatives, verify etc. there may be instances where there is no search for candidates beyond what the model generated originally; we also tried distilling forward-thinking traces but it showed the same trend (Appendix E). We leave the problem of designing synthetic or appropriate thinking traces for creative/open-ended problems to future work. Our model achieves win-rate of 68.3% against the gold idea, compared to 18.3% for GIANTS4B. We want to note that GIANTS was trained on similarity to gold-idea metric, which does not lead to the model generating ideas better than the gold idea (18.3% win rate) and also leads to collapse of ideas. sections.title: 6 DOWNSTREAM VALIDATION OF IDEA SETS
sections.content: To validate that the ideas generated by our model are actually promising for researchers, we conduct two experiments: (a) human study with domain experts and, (b) execution-based evaluation using coding agents.

sections.title: 6.1 HUMAN STUDY: PORTFOLIO QUALITY AND DIVERSITY
sections.content: We conduct pilot user study to evaluate if the ideas are usable, promising and unique to humans. To recruit users, we set minimum criterion that they have PhD in the field of NLP and at least four published academic papers in top-tier conferences. We onboard four participants for the task, that meet our established criteria. Each user gives us preference for the topics within NLP/ML they are comfortable with (self-declared expertise), and we match them with subset of queries from our test set that fall under those topics. Each user gets assigned 15 instances and they blind evaluate sets of ideas from three systems: Claude Opus 4.8, Qwen3-8B and our Proposed (no think) model. Overall, each user gives judgments on 45 sets of ideas. For each set of ideas, our experts make three judgments: (1) which ideas are worth pursuing as earlystage research directions (promising); (2) ignoring quality, the largest subset of ideas that pursue substantively different directions (unique); and (3) the same subset, restricted to ideas marked worth pursuing (Unique Promising). Two ideas count as the same direction when carrying out one would largely address the other. Generally, higher score is better for all these metrics. Results Table 4 reports aggregate judgments across 4 annotators and 60 instances. Our models portfolios contain 2.17 promising ideas and 2.83 unique ideas on average, against 2.20 and 2.72 for Claude Opus 4.8 and 1.52 and 2.52 for Qwen3-8B. Combining these, we see that our proposed model and Claude Opus 4.8 are considered similarly promising. Appendix breaks these results down by topics of the target paper and users.

sections.title: 7 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Quality and diversity in LLMs. large body of work has quantified the quality-diversity tradeoff in LLMs, across creative writing, open-ended generation, and idea generation (Zhang et al., 2025; Shypula et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Wadhwa et al., 2026; Padmakumar & He, 2024; Jiang et al., 2025). common finding is that RL and preference tuning collapse the policy onto few modes, trading diversity for quality (Kirk et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025). Training-time fixes reward diversity across independent rollouts of prompt (Li et al., 2025), or, in preference optimization, select diverse preference pairs (Lanchantin et al., 2026). More recent work rewards set of outputs directly, either to cover verifiable answer set (Puri et al., 2026) or to trade off fixed reward vector (Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026). All of these need an answer set or fixed reward space to define coverage. In open-ended ideation neither exists, since whether two ideas are distinct is itself judgment made in the context of the others in the set. Our objective addresses this by scoring each idea against the ones already written in the same generation. Research ideation. Literature-grounded ideation systems generally start from small seed and build ideas outward from it. SciMON (Wang et al., 2024) revises an idea until it is sufficiently novel relative to prior papers, ResearchAgent (Baek et al., 2025) refines proposal through rounds of reviewer feedback, and Nova generates hundreds of candidates from seed paper and clusters them to select diverse final set (Hu et al., 2025). Revision, critique, and clustering are all ways to obtain diversity, but they act after generation on candidates written without regard to one another, and the generator is never trained to write ideas that differ from each other. On the other hand, GIANTS (He-Yueya et al., 2026) trains model with RL to anticipate downstream papers core insight from its parent papers, and Tong et al. (2026) train judge and an ideator on community feedback such as citations, both rewarding one idea at time. separate line grounds ideation in execution, using the outcomes of implementing and running ideas as the reward. Si et al. (2026) find that reinforcement learning from execution signal suffers the model raises its average reward by converging on few simple ideas. from mode collapse: Because each idea is rewarded in isolation, nothing discourages repeating the same safe idea. We differ on both axes. Our input is whole body of documents instead of single seed, and the model writes set of ideas in one generation, trained on reward in which each idea is scored against the ones already written. We also use execution as an evaluation, checking whether sets of ideas succeed downstream (Section 6.2).

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present set-level RL objective for document-grounded ideation for training to generate diverse, high quality ideas. model is prompted/taught to generate ideas in one rollout and each ideas quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas before it. Our best 8B model (no think) achieves higher creative utility than strong closed-source models and competing quality-diversity objectives, while the think variant beats the closed-source models and is on par with DARLING. In small pilot human and execution studies its sets are comparable to Claude Opus 4.8s, so we see no evidence that diversity costs quality. Future work includes grounding-aware rewards, diversity across population, and reasoning traces designed for creative ideation. 9 Preprint. Under Review.

sections.title: LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our study currently focuses on scientific ideation based on context and parametric knowledge, instead of focusing on retrieval. This is partially because we are testing the set up of training with new set style generation where the aim is to increase diversity while also improving the quality. In future work we aim to include retrieval in this ideation process. We also train on english only, natural language processing scientific papers.

sections.content: A.1 DATA FORMAT In this Section we explain different aspects of the data curation process, including document acquisition, formats etc. Idea Format Each idea the model generates is JSON object in the four-field schema of Section 3. This includes: (problem gap, core claim, method, inspiration). The definitions of the four fields are given below (as per the inference prompt): problem gap: The gap the idea addresses, drawn from across the source documents an open question, tension, or unresolved difficulty that connects them and that none resolves on its own. State it as one clear gap, NOT as your specific solution to it. BEGIN this field with the single best-fitting OPPORTUNITY PATTERN label in square brackets (from the taxonomy below), then the prose gap (1 to 2 sentences). Pick the ONE dominant pattern even if several apply; if NONE genuinely fits, use [Other] rather than forcing poor match. Example: [Bridge Opportunity] Work on and on each..but neither connects... core claim: The couple of sentences the whole idea lives or dies on we claim that X. It must be something that could turn out to be wrong: definite, testable assertion / hypothesis / insight, not topic or direction. Do not just restate the gap, and do not describe what you would do about it. From these sentences alone reader should know exactly what the idea is betting on (1-2 sentences). method: At high level, how the claim would be turned into research the kind of move (combining ideas, extending to new setting, deriving formally, building an artifact, etc.) and how it addresses the gap. proposed approach, not step-by-step protocol. Begins with one bracketed Method Paradigm label. inspiration: Three to five sentences arguing how the idea arises FROM the source documents the relationship between them, not per-document restatement. Must (1) name each cited sources limitation and (2) justify why connecting them is non-obvious leap. Evaluation. At test time we sample three independent generations per instance and treat them as the set, since the policy was trained to produce one idea per generation. All metrics in Section 5 are computed on this set with the same judges as for the other models. B.4 OLMO-3 DETAILS To test that the recipe is not specific to one model family, we repeat it on Olmo-3-7B (Olmo et al., 2025). We initialize from allenai/Olmo-3-7B-Think-SFT, and run the same SFT (with and without thinking) and GRPO settings as Table 7. The length penalty is measured with the Olmo tokenizer. The two tokenizers count the card text within about 0.5%, so L0 is unchanged. Results are in Appendix (Transfer of recipe to other models). B.5 COMPUTE All runs use single node with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. SFT uses all 8 GPUs and takes about 46 minutes per epoch on 7,172 instances. For GRPO, 6 GPUs hold the policy and the vLLM rollouts, and 2 GPUs serve SciJudge-30B (tensor parallel size 2); the gpt-oss-120b distance judge is served through an external API and needs no local GPUs. GRPO step takes about one minute, so one epoch (about 600 steps at 12 prompts per step) takes roughly 10 hours. 17 Preprint. Under Review.

sections.content: win-rate Validating Quality. We validate the impact judge (Eq. 3) two ways: (i) validation against realworld papers (ii) robustness to length. (i) Agreement with real-world impact. We draw from our training set, papers from 2022 and 2023 and form pairs the same calendar year (within four months, to remove the age-of-paper confound). We only keep pairs that differ in their citation ratio (which we get from Semantic Scholar). We filter for citation ratio of 3 with absolute gap of at least 10 citations. To ensure the gap reflects meaningful use, we add an influential-citation gate (both papers influential-citation counts > 0, winner above loser by margin 5, we get this from Semantic Scholar). We rewrite each instance in the pair into idea-only summaries that reveal no results, metrics, or titles; the judge then compares ideas, and the higher-uptake paper is the gold winner. This yields 122 labeled pairs (244 papers). We ask the judge which idea is higher impact. For validation we only prompt the model once and report the strict win rate (no ties). On the idea-card format used throughout the paper, the evaluation judge GPT-5.4-mini picks the higher-impact idea 74% of the time. The training-reward judge SciJudge-30B, scores 65%  (Table 8)  . Between Claude and GPT, we went ahead with the latter for cost reasons. Because the reward is evaluated on every rollout during RL, its judge is queried orders of magnitude more often than the evaluation judge, which is applied once per test instance. We therefore optimize against smaller, cheaper judge and reserve stronger judge for evaluation. (ii) Robustness to length. To rule out that the judge merely prefers longer ideas, we summarize each candidate idea down to the gold ideas length (around 250 tokens) without changing its content and re-judge  (Table 9)  . Why not reward grounding? We do not put grounding in the training reward, for two reasons. First, optimizing three objectives in one run proved unstable. In our initial runs, grounding entered the reward as graded multiplier and later as binary gate, and the policy gamed the judges category preferences (for example, the grounding-type distribution collapsed onto single type). Second, grounding has no natural direction in which higher is always better. Our score measures how much an idea depends on its cited sources, so highly grounded idea can be simple, incremental extension of them, while less grounded one can be promising departure that is only loosely motivated by the documents. We therefore instruct the model at the prompt level to name the sources each idea draws on (Appendix A.1), and track grounding separately as diagnostic (Section 5). This is limitation of our objective: some drop in grounding is expected when ideas move away from their sources, but the drop after RL  (Table 11)  is large, because nothing in the reward penalizes drifting, and finding stable way to enforce floor is future work. Maximizing over orderings is combinatorial, so, following CREATE, we approximate it with the greedy (farthest-point) order: take the highest-quality idea first, then repeatedly take the idea with the largest marginal value q(u) minjpicked d(u, uj).
